questions.question: State the law of electric charges. Two balloons rubbed on wool are hung side by side and then the wool is brought near. Explain what is observed and state two factors that affect the size of the force.
questions.expected_answer: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Both balloons gain electrons from the wool and become negative; like charges repel, so the balloons swing apart. The wool loses electrons and becomes positive; unlike charges attract, so each balloon swings towards the wool. The force is larger when the charges are larger (e.g. more vigorous rubbing) and when the objects are closer together; it weakens rapidly as the distance increases (doubling the distance gives a quarter of the force).

questions.question: Explain, using induced charge separation, why a negatively charged comb attracts small neutral pieces of paper, and why some pieces jump away after touching the comb.
questions.expected_answer: The negative comb repels electrons in the paper slightly away and attracts the positive parts slightly closer, so the side of the paper nearest the comb becomes slightly positive and the far side slightly negative, though the paper stays neutral overall. Because the positive side is closer, the attraction to it is stronger than the repulsion of the further negative side, so there is a net attraction and the paper is lifted. When a piece touches the comb, some negative charge transfers to it; it now has the same charge as the comb, and like charges repel, so it jumps away.

questions.question: Describe how an electroscope detects charge and how it can identify the sign of an unknown charge. Describe one industrial use of electrostatic forces.
questions.expected_answer: A gold-leaf electroscope has a metal cap, rod, plate and thin gold leaf in a glass case. When a charged object touches (or is brought near) the cap, charge spreads (or is pushed) to the plate and leaf, giving them the same charge, so they repel and the leaf rises. To find the sign: charge the electroscope with a known charge (e.g. negative); bring the unknown near the cap; if the leaf rises further, the object has the same charge; if it falls, it has the opposite charge (or may be neutral). Industrial use: electrostatic spray painting — paint droplets are charged and the car body is earthed or oppositely charged, so the droplets spread evenly and are attracted onto the car, wasting little paint. (Also precipitators: charged ash particles are attracted to oppositely charged plates.)
